title: Ley de Presupuesto 2026: déficit de realismo | Diario Financiero
content: The 2026 Budget Law project continues the pattern of overly optimistic income projections seen in the previous two years, with a fiscal overestimation of approximately US$4.5 billion in revenue. Although projected expenditures for this year are slightly lower than those included in the Budget Law, actual spending moderation is estimated at around US$1 billion, primarily due to reduced capital transfers. Current spending has grown by 2.6% in real terms through August, in line with projections. However, when actual revenues fall short of estimates, spending cuts disproportionately affect investment. For 2026, income forecasts remain optimistic but less so than in prior years, projecting a 5% real increase in tax revenues compared to 2025, despite a 2.5% real GDP growth—indicating a high elasticity, likely driven by the Tax Compliance Law. This 5% projection assumes a 10% real tax revenue increase from September to December 2025 compared to the same period in 2024, which is unlikely given that tax revenues had already grown by 7.7% in real terms through August. Thus, actual fiscal revenues for 2025 are likely to fall short of projections, making the 2026 estimates even more ambitious. As a result, the Budget Law's assumptions are still unrealistic, increasing the likelihood that both the effective and cyclical-adjusted deficit will exceed the projected 1.5% and 1.1% targets for 2026, mirroring the outcomes of 2023, 2024, and 2025.

title: ABD korkutmaya başladı... Ekonomisi çökecek mi?
content: The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) estimates that the US federal budget deficit will be approximately $1 trillion higher than previously predicted over the next 10 years. According to the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB), the cumulative deficit from 2026 to 2035 will reach $22.7 trillion, surpassing the CBO's January estimate of $21.8 trillion. The new projections take into account the effects of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which included comprehensive tax cuts and increased spending during the Trump administration. CRFB estimates that this law alone will increase deficits by $4.6 trillion by 2035. However, the new tariffs implemented by Trump are expected to generate approximately $3.4 trillion in revenue over the next decade, which could help offset some of the deficits. CRFB also predicts a budget deficit of $1.7 trillion for the 2025 fiscal year, which is slightly lower than the previous year. However, deficits are expected to increase over time, reaching $2.6 trillion by 2035, equivalent to 5.9% of GDP. Interest payments are also expected to rise rapidly, from approximately $1 trillion in 2025 to $1.8 trillion in 2035, totaling $14 trillion over the 10-year period. In a more pessimistic scenario, if courts were to invalidate tariffs, some temporary tax cuts were to become permanent, and interest rates were to remain high, deficits could increase by $7 trillion and the debt-to-GDP ratio could reach 134% by 2035, posing a significant risk to the country's fiscal sustainability.

title: 图解美国2025财年：关税收入大增，债务利息破万亿
content: The 2025 U.S. fiscal year saw a change in presidential administration, but the country's fiscal situation remained严峻, according to the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) data released on October 10, 2025. Despite record-high tariff revenues, the federal budget deficit remained unchanged compared to the previous fiscal year. This stagnation is largely due to ongoing increases in major spending drivers, including Social Security, Medicare, and public debt interest. Notably, public debt interest expenditures surpassed $1 trillion for the first time, according to one metric. The CBO's year-end report highlighted five key insights into the U.S. government's fiscal condition for the 2025 fiscal year, which ended on September 30, 2025.

title: Year-End Tax Planning 2025
content: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), signed into law in July 2025, introduces sweeping federal tax reforms with significant implications for American taxpayers. Individual income tax brackets (10% to 37%) are now permanent, providing stability for high earners above $626,350 (single) or $751,600 (joint). The standard deduction increases to $15,000 for single filers and $30,000 for joint filers, with inflation adjustments built in, reducing the incentive to itemize. The SALT deduction cap rises to $40,000 for 2025 but phases out for higher earners and reverts to $10,000 in 2030. The unified lifetime gift, estate, and generation-skipping transfer exemption permanently increases to $15 million per person ($30 million per couple) starting in 2026, indexed for inflation. The annual gift tax exclusion is $19,000 per recipient, enabling strategic wealth transfer. Section 1202 Qualified Small Business Stock exclusion increases to $15 million or 10x basis after five years, with partial exclusions at three and four years. Opportunity Zones become permanent, with expanded benefits in 2027. 'Trump Accounts for Kids' allow up to $5,000 annual contributions for minors born 2025–2028, with government matching. Charitable giving limitations take effect in 2026: only gifts exceeding 0.5% of AGI qualify, with itemized deductions capped at 35% for high earners—creating a strong incentive to 'bunch' donations in 2025. IRA charitable distributions up to $108,000 are allowed for those aged 70+, satisfying required minimum distributions tax-free. The 20% Section 199A QBI deduction becomes permanent with expanded eligibility. Section 179 immediate expensing increases to $2.5 million for qualifying business purchases. New above-the-line deductions are available for tip income (up to $25,000), overtime pay (up to $12,500), and passenger vehicle loan interest (up to $10,000), subject to income limits. These changes create broad opportunities—but also risks—requiring proactive planning before December 31, 2025, to capture long-term benefits. According to Forbes, taxpayers are urged to consult qualified advisors before implementing strategies.

title: 2026年美联邦税改出炉 如何影响个人和家庭 | IRS | 国税局 | 美国国税局 | 大纪元
content: The U.S. Internal Revenue Service (IRS) released the 2026 tax inflation adjustment announcement on October 9, 2025, outlining significant changes from the 'One Big Beautiful Bill Act' signed by President Trump in July 2025. These adjustments will affect tax returns filed in 2027 and potential refund amounts. For the 2026 tax year, the Child Tax Credit (CTC) maximum was raised to $2,200 per qualifying child, up from $2,000, with the refundable portion remaining at $1,700. The Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) saw increases across all categories: $8,231 (up from $8,046) for three or more children, $7,316 (up from $7,152) for two children, $4,427 (up from $4,328) for one child, and $664 (up from $649) for those with no children. EITC phase-out thresholds were set at $70,224 (married filing jointly, three or more children) and $62,974 (single, three or more children), among others. Investment income over $12,200 disqualifies taxpayers from EITC. Adoption Credit maximum rose to $17,670 (from $17,280), with a refundable portion of $5,120. The annual gift exclusion remains at $19,000, but the exclusion for gifts to non-U.S. citizen spouses increased to $194,000 (up $4,000 from 2025). The IRS confirmed that the $2,200 CTC cap will be indexed to inflation starting in 2027.

content: The U.S. Internal Revenue Service (IRS) released the 2026 tax inflation adjustments on October 9, 2025, with changes effective for tax returns filed in 2027. These updates stem from the 'One Big Beautiful Bill Act' signed by President Trump in July, which increased the Child Tax Credit (CTC) maximum to $2,200 per qualifying child, up from $2,000, effective in 2025 and 2026. The refundable portion of the CTC remains at $1,700 for 2026. The Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) was also increased: $8,231 for three or more children (up from $8,046), $7,316 for two children (up from $7,152), $4,427 for one child (up from $4,328), and $664 for no children (up from $649). EITC eligibility phases out at adjusted gross income (AGI) levels of $70,224 (married filing jointly, three+ children), $65,899 (two children), $58,863 (one child), and $26,820 (no children); for single filers, the phase-out thresholds are $62,974, $58,629, $51,593, and $19,540, respectively. Investment income over $12,200 disqualifies taxpayers from EITC. Adoption credit maximums rose to $17,670 (from $17,280), with a refundable portion of $5,120. The annual gift exclusion remains $19,000, but the exclusion for gifts to non-U.S. citizen spouses increased to $194,000 (up $4,000 from 2025). These changes are expected to impact individual and family tax liabilities and refund amounts.

title: US annual budget deficit steady at $1.8 trillion, despite surge in tariff revenue
content: The U.S. federal government recorded a $1.8 trillion budget deficit for the 2025 fiscal year, according to the Congressional Budget Office (CBO), a figure nearly unchanged from the $1.808 trillion deficit in 2024. Despite a $308 billion (6%) increase in revenues—driven largely by $195 billion in tariff revenues under President Donald Trump’s trade policies, up from $77 billion in 2024—spending rose by $301 billion (4%), primarily due to interest on the public debt surpassing $1 trillion for the first time. Corporate tax receipts fell 15% compared to 2024, partly due to a July 2025 tax and spending plan that expanded investment deductions and a deferral of revenue from 2023 to 2024. Social Security spending increased by $121 billion (8%) due to cost-of-living adjustments and new legislation. Meanwhile, Department of Education spending dropped by $234 billion (87%), largely due to changes in student loan accounting and an executive order in March 2025 to shutter many of its functions. The CBO did not provide a deficit-to-GDP ratio, but using its September GDP forecast, the ratio was estimated at 5.9%, down from 6.4% in 2024. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent aims to reduce the ratio to 3% by 2028. The CBO report was released amid a federal government shutdown, which may delay the official Treasury release of the September and 2025 fiscal-year data.

content: The U.S. federal government collected more than double the tariff revenue in the 2025 fiscal year compared to the previous year, amounting to $195 billion (approximately 277 trillion KRW), according to estimates from the Congressional Budget Office reported by The Wall Street Journal. However, this increase was partly due to the implementation of higher tariffs starting in April 2024, which limited the year-over-year growth rate. Despite the rise in tariff income, the U.S. government's interest payments on public debt surged to $1.29 trillion—exceeding $1 trillion for the first time—representing an 8% increase from the prior year. This rise is attributed to growing public debt and rising interest rates. Interest expenses now surpass spending on Medicare and defense, consuming roughly $1 of every $5 in tax revenue. The projected fiscal deficit for the 2025 fiscal year is $1.8 trillion, nearly unchanged from the previous year. The debt-to-GDP ratio is estimated to be near 100%, while the deficit-to-GDP ratio declined slightly from 6.4% in 2024 to 5.9% in 2025.

title: US public debt to rise from 100% of GDP now to 120% by 2035: CRFB
content: The Congressional Research Service’s Fiscal Outlook (CRFB) projects that U.S. deficits over the next decade will total $22.7 trillion, or 6.1 % of GDP, rising from $1.7 trillion (5.6 % of GDP) in 2025 to $2.6 trillion (5.9 % of GDP) in 2035. Net interest payments on the national debt will reach $14.0 trillion (3.8 % of GDP), up from nearly $1 trillion (3.2 % of GDP) in 2025 to $1.8 trillion (4.1 % of GDP) in 2035. Spending is projected at $88 trillion (23.6 % of GDP) while revenue is estimated at $65 trillion (17.5 % of GDP). These estimates are based on the CRFB adjusted August 2025 baseline, which assumes current tariffs and trade deals remain in effect. The report notes that total deficits are about $1 trillion higher than the Congressional Budget Office’s January baseline, with debt‑to‑GDP rising by an extra 2 percentage points. In an alternative scenario—if the U.S. Trade Court upholds the illegality of many tariffs, makes temporary provisions of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act permanent, and treasury yields stay unchanged—debt could reach 134 % of GDP, the ten‑year deficit would exceed $28 trillion, and interest payments would rise to $2.2 trillion by 2035, above 5 % of GDP. "Total deficits are about $1 trillion higher than in the Congressional Budget Office's (CBO) January baseline, with debt‑to‑GDP rising by an extra 2 percentage points," the CRFB release said.
